title: Air-gapped bootstrapping, transport & checksum playbook (draft)
purpose: This is an operational playbook + terraform module notes for bootstrapping Redwood Private in air-gapped / disconnected customer environments. Focus areas: artifact bundle composition, secure transport (sneakernet / registry-proxy), signed-file verification (SFV), offline registry layout, and an upgrade window checklist for minor/major releases.
scope: Applies to VPC and on-prem installs that have no direct outbound access to public container registries or Redwood-hosted artifact repositories.
Intended for SRE/Platform engineers and Solutions Engineers running installs for customers or producing offline bundles.
Not a substitute for the formal on-site runbook; this is a living draft for module authors and release engineers.
assumptions: Customer can accept physical media (USB / external SSD) or has an approved pull-through proxy in an isolated network.
Customer manages a KMS or can provide a GPG key to verify signatures.
Release artifacts are produced by the build pipeline and stored in a staging registry accessible to our release engineers.
bundle composition (recommended minimal: container-images.tar.gz: tar of all OCI images (manifest + blobs) exported with skopeo or crane for the release tag.
charts-and-helm-values.tar.gz: customer-specific overlay charts and default values used during install.
tf-modules.tar.gz: compiled terraform modules (if we include prepackaged providers/providers .zip and registry metadata).
signature-manifest.sfv: newline-separated list of files and SHA256 checksums + detached GPG signatures for each major artifact.
version-manifest.txt: semver, image digests mapping (image_name -> sha256:... ), release notes excerpt.
install.sh (or install.ps1): simple orchestrator that performs preflight checks and extracts artifacts locally.
signing & verification (SFV pattern):
We use an SFV-style manifest: each line: <sha256sum>  <relpath>
Each artifact also has a detached signature: <artifact>.sig (GPG signed with release key).
Verification workflow (operator steps):
  - import Redwood public key (or customer-provided key) into GPG keyring
  - gpg --verify signature-manifest.sfv.sig signature-manifest.sfv
  - sha256sum -c signature-manifest.sfv  (run in the bundle root)
Failure semantics: any checksum mismatch aborts install; record artifact, device serial and contact release-engineering.
offline registry layout (recommended):
layout/
  - index.yaml (simple listing of images and tags)
  - images/ (blobs imported via crane or skopeo)
  - manifests/ (oci manifests to allow regctl/registry import)
If customer will run a local registry (Harbor/Quay), provide a registry import script using 'crane push' or 'regctl image import'.
transport options and tradeoffs:
sneakernet (recommended for totally sealed sites):
  - pros: simple, audit-friendly, no network config required.
  - cons: human error, slower iteration, needs checksum+signature verification strictly enforced.
  - logistics: label device, record SHA256 of device image set, use tamper-evident seals.
one-way physical import with proxy staging host:
  - pros: faster installs, can centralize verification.
  - cons: requires a staging host inside customer perimeter and a trusted operator.
inbound registry pull via temporary VPN/bastion (least preferred):
  - pros: fastest for updates.
  - cons: security approvals, complex firewall rules, audit surface increases.
terraform module notes (interface + idem:
Goal: provide a small module set that can be executed without external provider downloads at apply-time.
Module: redwood_airgap_bundle
  - inputs (recommended):
    - bundle_path (string): local path on operator machine or path on staging host
    - registry_host (string): hostname of local registry to seed
    - tls_skip_verify (bool): default false (only for trusted staging hosts)
    - image_tag_map (map): optional remap of image names -> <registry_host>/<repo>@sha256:...
    - gpg_key_fingerprint (string): optional; if provided, module will verify signatures before seeding
  - outputs:
    - seeded_images (list): image reference list successfully pushed to registry
    - seeding_report_url (string): if using queued background job to seed, provide path to report
Implementation notes:
  - Avoid remote state downloads of provider binaries: vendor terraform providers in tf-modules.tar.gz or instruct operators how to install provider plugins on the CLI host.
  - Module should be idempotent: re-running with same bundle should be a no-op after successful seed; use local marker files (e.g., /var/lib/redwood/airgap/seeding-record.json) with signed digest to avoid repeated work.
  - Prefer convergent operations: attempt to validate image existence via registry APIs before attempting push.
upgrade plan (minor and major release pa:
pre-upgrade window checklist (complete these 48–2 hours before window):
  - collect current manifest: kubectl get pods, deployments, and redwood version API
  - snapshot PVs (if any stateful components) and backup etcd/metadata
  - verify current SFV manifest and that bundle for target release is intact
  - smoke test: deploy a canary subset (1% traffic or single node) in an isolated namespace
  - confirm rollback artifacts exist (previous images and helm charts)
rolling upgrade steps (recommended):
  - 1) seed offline registry if new images present
  - 2) upgrade infra (CRDs, helm charts) in canary namespace
  - 3) run integration smoke tests (llm-e2e quick prompt + embedding sanity)
  - 4) progress to 25% / 50% / 100% rollout with 15m observation windows
  - 5) if any SR error rates exceed thresholds (defined locally), run rollback path
rollback strategy:
  - use pinned image digests (not tags) to redeploy previous revision
  - restore any changed ConfigMaps or helm values from versioned backups
  - in severe cases, restore PV snapshots and re-apply previous helm release
preflight & health checks (automated): registry readiness: check /v2/_catalog and registry storage space > 2x expected bundle
nodes: disk space > 20% free on nodes hosting image cache
network: MTU mismatch detection for customer VPNs (common cause of large layer push failures)
service health: sample inference job (1k tokens) should complete under configured latency SLO on canary
observability & telemetry during install:
enable verbose install logs to a local file and upload to support bundle if contactless support enabled
collect kube events, containerd logs, and regctl output
seed a minimal Prometheus scrape job pointing at critical components for 30m retention
post-install verification (must-pass): ingest example prompt and verify output checksum against expected hash (where feasible)
validate embeddings pipeline with simple dataset (sample 100 vectors) and check counts
run cross-version smoke tests (regression checks) from release-evals suite
manual troubleshooting quick hits:
common failure: "layer push rejected: blob unknown"
  - likely: missing manifest or wrong registry namespace mapping; re-run manifest import with regctl
common failure: GPG error on signature verification
  - inspect gpg --list-keys, verify fingerprint matches release key, check timezone skew and file corruption
operational run cadence & responsibiliti: release-engineering: produce bundle, sign SFV, upload to secure staging, open JIRA with artifact digests
solutions-engineering: coordinate physical transfer and customer point-of-contact
customer-platform: perform seeding and install; provide logs and run preflight checks
support: retain contact window during upgrade + 4 hours after completion
open questions / decisions needed:
Should we include pre-built terraform providers in every bundle or a separate 'tooling' USB with provider binaries? pros/cons listed above — decision required from infra-plat team.
Do customers prefer GPG detached signatures or a PKI-based timestamped manifest (Sigstore)? Migration strategy needs exploration; Sigstore would simplify key management but customer network policies may block it.
Migration from existing "sneakernet" artifacts to a long-term registry mirror service — needs pricing/ops sign-off.
